questions.text: In this lesson’s dual-era client, why is a discovery timeout insufficient evidence to select legacy behavior?

options.A: Because timeouts prove the peer supports modern request metadata.
options.B: Because every legacy server must respond to discovery successfully.
options.C: Because a timeout means initialization has already completed.
options.D: Because overload or transport failure can produce the same signal.

questions.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous. Legacy selection requires explicit permission to probe plus a valid positive initialize result for a supported legacy revision.

questions.text: An allowlisted peer returns the recognized modern error -32022 with a mutually supported version. What should the lesson’s client do next?

options.A: Send initialize because the legacy allowlist overrides the error.
options.B: Retry modern discovery using that version and a new request ID.
options.C: Resend the identical request with the same unsupported version.
options.D: Select legacy behavior immediately without a positive probe result.

questions.explanation: A recognized modern version error proves modern behavior. The client selects a mutual modern version and retries with a new ID; it does not downgrade.

questions.text: Both files and notes advertise search, and merge() uses its default policy. With peers processed alphabetically, what does call("notes/search", {}) send?

options.A: A tools/call to files with name="notes/search".
options.B: A tools/call to notes with name="notes/search".
options.C: A tools/call to notes with name="search".
options.D: A tools/call to both peers with name="search".

questions.explanation: The merged registry stores notes/search as the canonical name with peer_name notes and local_name search. call routes to the owning peer using the local name.
